thread.title: Follow the money — the mark-to-market grade for the Trump administration isn’t great - MarketWatch

author: Paul Brandus
title: Follow the money — the mark-to-market grade for the Trump administration isn’t great - MarketWatch
text:
MANDEL NGAN/AFP/Getty Images US President Donald Trump (L) shakes hands with Steven Mnuchin. One way to curb global warming is for politicians to talk less. So much hot air comes out of their mouths, I’ll bet it’s linked to the melting of the polar ice caps.
Take Treasury Steven Mnuchin. In February 2017 he was asked on CNBC if he saw the rising stock market as a “report card” on the Trump administration.
“Absolutely,” he said, without even waiting for the question to be finished. “This is a mark-to-market business, and you see what the market thinks.”
Donald Trump had only been president for a month, and already Mnuchin was handing out grades.
What might that grade be now? With the S&P 500 SPX, +0.21% , Dow DJIA, +0.10% and Nasdaq COMP, +0.84% down 10.4.%, 9.5% and 14.3%, respectively (as of the Friday close), judge for yourself.
Now while it’s true, as J.P. Morgan famously said more than a century ago, that “the market is going to fluctuate,” it’s worth asking just why—after rising sharply since March 2009—it’s so volatile now. Some reasons are perfectly normal. Interest rates have been rising; higher rates tend to make equities less attractive on a relative basis. And there are concerns that corporate profit growth, while still increasing, may be losing steam. And so forth. These are normal parts of an economic cycle.
But there are other reasons this time around that are far from normal. The administration’s trade war is the principal reason. Trump has disrupted supply chains, blown up market relationships that took years to build—just ask Midwest farmers—and added uncertainty that makes executives cautious about capital spending, and foreign investors think twice about investing in America.
But don’t take my word for it, just follow the money. On the first point, capital spending, consider this: Trump and Mnuchin boasted that corporate tax cuts would mean huge investment and growth in the U.S. economy. It hasn’t worked out that way. According to data compiled by New York investment bank Westwood Capital , just 28.6% of business investment has gone to “structures and industrial equipment” this year. Twenty years ago, at the end of another U.S. expansion, nearly half—48.3%—did.
Instead, the bulk of U.S. business investment now—52%—has gone into things like technology and intellectual property, which create value—just look at the long-term stock market gains of tech giants like Apple AAPL, +0.75% , Amazon AMZN, +0.73% and Microsoft MSFT, +2.43% —but not jobs.
This isn’t the administration’s fault; manufacturing, as a percentage of U.S. jobs, peaked just after World War II. But its claim that tax cuts would spark a robust manufacturing revival simply hasn’t panned out. A modest boost, perhaps—but one set against a much larger trend that continues to go the opposite way.
Speaking of jobs, some 6.8 million Americans work for a foreign employer (2015 data), so tracking foreign investment in the United States is more than a mere academic task. Foreign companies invest here when conditions are good, and when uncertainty is minimized. Let’s follow the money once again.
Here’s how much foreigners have invested in the United States in recent years:
2015: $482 billion
2016: $486 billion
But what happened in 2017? That figure plunged to $292 billion, a drop of 40%. Preliminary data shows it falling further this year. There are several reasons for this, acknowledges the Organization for International Investment, a Washington-based trade group that represents U.S. subsidiaries of overseas corporations. Yet one of them is undeniable: It is, the report says, “a response to import tariffs and other trade actions from the Trump Administration as international companies hit the pause button on potential investments.”
And that means jobs.
If the stock market can be judged as a report card, this can too. Millions of Americans jobs depend on foreigners having confidence in America, and when that confidence is wobbly, as it is now, that capital shifts elsewhere. People who say who cares what a bunch of foreigners think aren’t thinking themselves.
When confidence lags, when uncertainty reigns, the markets suffer. It’s as simple as that. The markets sank because investors decided that the dinner between Trump and Chinese President Xi apparently didn’t do much resolve their trade dispute. It’s also not helpful when the president himself—who has now taken to calling himself “tariff man”—keeps demonstrating his ignorance about tariffs. “We’re collecting billions!” he gushes, not seeming to realize that tariffs are generally paid by the end user—consumers. Tariffs are nothing more than a tax on the American people. Why is Trump bragging about raising taxes? In my book, that’s a failing grade.
Paul Brandus Paul Brandus is the White House bureau chief for West Wing Reports. You can follow him on Twitter WestWingReport .
